A total of 97,082 dengue patients have so far been hospitalized across the country this year, according to the DGHS report.
However, in the last 24 hours, 1,627 patients recovered and were discharged from hospitals.
So far, 91,007 dengue patients have recovered and returned home after receiving treatment this year.
A total of 102,861 people were infected with dengue, and 413 people died from the disease last year.

item.title: Bangladesh discusses €250 million loan for women's health initiative
item.description:
Bangladesh discussed a proposed €250 million loan from the European Investment Bank (EIB) to implement a women's health initiative with international development partners during the World Health Summit (WHS) 2026 in Berlin, Germany, on Saturday.
The bilateral and technical discussions took place at the Charité campus in Berlin, involving a high-level delegation from the Bangladesh government and international development partners.
The Bangladesh delegation was led by Health and Family Welfare Minister Sardar Md Sakhawat Husain and Special Assistant to the Prime Minister on Health Ziauddin Hyder.
The proposed Women's Health Initiative aims to reduce maternal mortality, ensure early detection of cervical and breast cancers, and develop modern facilities to provide round-the-clock emergency obstetric services at the union level.
The discussions also covered strengthening district hospitals and introducing a digital patient-tracking system.
The United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA), Charité – Universitätsmedizin Berlin, and the Berlin Institute of Health (BIH) are providing technical and strategic support for the initiative.
Health and Family Welfare Minister Sardar Md Sakhawat Husain said: “This international partnership will play an important role in ensuring quality healthcare for women and girls in remote areas of Bangladesh.”
The Bangladesh delegation also visited Charité Hospital in Berlin to observe its medical facilities and cancer screening services.
The parties agreed to form a joint working group to support the future development of healthcare systems in both countries.

item.title: Abdul Awal Mintoo: Bangladesh, India to hold talks on elephant corridor in Sherpur
item.description:
Environment, Forest and Climate Change Minister Abdul Awal Mintoo on Saturday said the government would soon initiate talks with India under an existing protocol to establish a cross-border corridor for wild elephants roaming the Garo Hills in Sherpur.
Around 130 to 135 wild elephants that came from India's Meghalaya have become stranded in the Garo Hills of Sherpur as border fencing has prevented them from returning to their habitat, he said.
The minister said the government would request the Indian authorities to open gates in the fencing to allow the elephants to return, although previous requests had not received a positive response.
At the same time, initiatives would be taken to develop forest areas in Sherpur into safe habitats for the elephants, he added.
The minister made the remarks while speaking at a discussion on resolving human-elephant conflict and conserving wild elephants at Madhutila Eco Park in Nalitabari upazila of Sherpur.
He said the scenic Garo Hills, its wild elephants and the surrounding natural environment would be used to develop the area into a tourism hub. This would create economic opportunities for local people while helping protect elephants and reduce human-elephant conflict, he added.
The Sherpur district administration and the Mymensingh Forest Division organized the discussion with lawmakers from elephant-affected areas, Elephant Response Team (ERT) members, journalists and volunteers involved in elephant conservation. Deputy Commissioner Farida Yesmin chaired the event.
Sherpur-2 lawmaker Engineer Fahim Chowdhury, Chief Conservator of Forests Md Amir Hossain Chowdhury, Conservator of Forests for the Wildlife and Nature Conservation Region Md Sanaullah Patwari, Central Region Conservator of Forests ASM Zahir Uddin Akon, Mymensingh Divisional Forest Officer Kazi Muhammad Nurul Karim and Police Superintendent AKM Johirul Islam spoke as special guests.

item.title: YouTuber Dhruv Rathee detained by Delhi Police; CJP demands release
item.description:
YouTuber Dhruv Rathee was detained by Delhi Police at his residence in Gurugram’s Sector 56 on Saturday ahead of the Cockroach Janta Party’s (CJP) planned protest at Jantar Mantar, NDTV reported, citing police sources.
Rathee had arrived to join the demonstration, prompting heightened security arrangements across the national capital.
According to sources, around 50 Delhi Police personnel arrived at Rathee’s Gurugram residence on Saturday morning and detained him.
The detention drew a sharp response from the CJP, which demanded his “immediate release”.
On Friday evening, Rathee announced his participation in Saturday’s protest in a video posted on his X account.
A vocal critic of the Narendra Modi government, Rathee arrived in India from Germany earlier this week and joined a CJP protest in Bengaluru on October 8.
Rathee has a substantial online following, with 19.2 million Instagram followers, 3.3 million on X, and 33 million YouTube subscribers.
Earlier this week, Delhi Police denied permission for the protest, citing security concerns and procedural requirements.
Police have stepped up preventive detentions and deployed personnel at strategic locations to prevent protesters from reaching the protest site.
More than 400 people were detained overnight, while hundreds of trains were cancelled and dozens of metro stations shut ahead of a large-scale protest against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar in central Delhi on Saturday.
The CJP mobilised supporters to gather at Jantar Mantar, while the Centre deployed more than 20,000 police and Central Armed Police Forces personnel to maintain law and order.

item.title: Tagore mural targeted outside Shilpakala Academy, one detained
item.description:
Police detained ANM Ayas, a leader of Rashtra Sanglap Forum, on Saturday afternoon for allegedly attempting to deface a mural of Nobel laureate Rabindranath Tagore outside Bangladesh Shilpakala Academy in the capital’s Segunbagicha area.
The incident occurred just five days after Dhaka South City Corporation (DSCC) cleared the footpath of encroachments and decorated an adjoining wall with portraits of 10 prominent figures from Bengali literature, art and culture.
Shahbag Police Station Sub-Inspector Abdul Khalek confirmed the detention, saying Ayas had been taken to the police station after attempting to erase Tagore’s portrait.
The incident comes amid criticism over the selection of cultural personalities featured in the murals, particularly the inclusion of figures from West Bengal and the absence of women.
According to reports, police intervened after an attempt was made to apply black or white paint to the portraits outside the academy.
The Daily Campus reported that three people, including Ayas, were detained in connection with the incident. Other reports initially confirmed only Ayas’s detention.
The Daily Campus also described Ayas as president of Rashtra Sanglap Forum, while other outlets identified him as its member secretary.
On October 5, DSCC reopened the Segunbagicha footpath following an operation to remove encroachments.
As part of the renovation, portraits of 10 cultural figures were painted on a roadside wall near Shilpakala Academy.
They included Rabindranath Tagore, national poet Kazi Nazrul Islam, Shilpacharya Zainul Abedin, filmmaker Satyajit Ray, philosopher and social reformer Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar, Fakir Lalon Shah, artist SM Sultan, filmmaker Zahir Raihan, folk singer Shah Abdul Karim and actor Humayun Faridi.
The project also included new dustbins, benches for pedestrians and repairs to the boundary wall.
The newly renovated stretch was opened to pedestrians after the removal of makeshift shops and other obstructions.
It was not immediately clear whether any formal case had been filed or what further legal action police intended to take.

item.title: PM assures support for waste-to-fuel technology
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on Saturday assured support for a technology that could turn waste into fuel oil and help reduce Bangladesh’s dependence on imported energy.
He gave the assurance as a team of researchers led by Khulna University of Engineering and Technology (Kuet) Professor Dr Md Khalequzzaman briefed him on the technology at his office in Tejgaon, said a release issued by the PM’s Press Wing.
The technology uses a process known as hydrothermal liquefaction (HTL) to convert human waste, waste from sewage treatment plants, kitchen waste and agricultural residues into fuel oil.
The researchers said they have been working on the technology for around 10 years and have achieved a 50–55% biocrude yield in laboratory tests. They have also made progress in producing biocrude with a high diesel content.
The next step is to set up a pilot plant capable of processing one to three tons of waste daily to assess the technology’s efficiency, production costs and commercial viability. The estimated cost of the pilot project is Tk100–120 crore.
According to the researchers, the technology, if developed for commercial-scale production, could replace around 10–15% of imported crude oil and save foreign currency equivalent to Tk6,500–13,000 crore annually.
However, the estimates would need to be validated through large-scale technical and economic assessments, they said.
The researchers said the technology could also help reduce environmental pollution, improve waste management and create opportunities for developing a domestic fuel industry.
The Prime Minister assured them of the government’s necessary cooperation in advancing the initiative.
Power and Energy Minister Iqbal Mahmood Tuku, State Minister Anindya Islam Amit, University Grants Commission member Professor Abdullah Al Mamun, Kuet Vice-Chancellor Professor Mohammad Masud and Bangladesh Petroleum Corporation Chairman Dr Mohammad Rafiqul Islam were present at the briefing.

item.title: CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke, two others detained aboard plane in Delhi
item.description:
Police detained Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) founder Abhijit Dipke and two other party members aboard an aircraft shortly after it landed at Delhi Airport, ahead of the party’s planned protest at Jantar Mantar, reports NDTV.
Dipke went live on Instagram as police entered the aircraft. The video shows officers detaining Dipke, Sourav Das and Ashutosh Ranka inside the plane.
The footage captures a commotion as CJP members questioned the police over their decision to detain them before passengers had disembarked.
In the video, Dipke is heard telling female police officers: “You could have waited for us to step out. Come, arrest us. We are not afraid.”

item.title: States told by Indian govt to stop protest march to Delhi
item.description:
India’s Union Ministry of Home Affairs has asked all states and Union Territories to coordinate with Delhi Police and take preventive measures to stop protesters from travelling to the national capital ahead of a planned demonstration by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), The Hindu reported.
In a letter to state chief secretaries and police chiefs on Friday, Union Home Secretary Govind Mohan flagged the “grave law and order and public order implications” of the planned protest at Jantar Mantar on Saturday.
The protesters are demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over concerns about the Election Commission’s functioning and its handling of the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.
Authorities have introduced sweeping restrictions ahead of the demonstration. These include preventive detentions, train cancellations, the closure of metro stations and the suspension of mobile internet services in parts of central Delhi.
The restrictions have drawn criticism from protest organisers, who have described the measures as intimidation by the authorities.
In its letter, the Union government said Delhi Police had rejected the organisers’ request to hold the demonstration at Jantar Mantar, ANI reported.
The ministry also cited what it described as a “documented history of non-compliance with lawful directions” by the CJP and organisations supporting it during an earlier protest. It alleged that the previous demonstration, involving participants from several states, had disrupted public order and damaged public property, The Hindu reported.
The ministry said intelligence inputs suggested that CJP members and supporters planned to defy prohibitory orders and enter Delhi through multiple routes.
It directed states and Union Territories to “immediately operationalise preventive measures” in coordination with Delhi Police to maintain public order and protect critical infrastructure.
The government also stressed the need for real-time intelligence sharing among state agencies, transit authorities and Delhi Police to ensure coordinated action.
The planned demonstration follows several days of protests by opposition INDIA bloc members in Delhi and other parts of India, calling for Kumar’s resignation over concerns about electoral roll revisions and the functioning of the Election Commission.

item.title: Mahatma Gandhi’s great-grandson detained in Mumbai ahead of CJP protest
item.description:
Mumbai Police detained Tushar Gandhi, great-grandson of Mahatma Gandhi and president of Hum Bharat Ke Log, along with his associates on Saturday as they headed to August Kranti Maidan for a protest in support of the Cockroach Janata Party’s (CJP) demonstration in Delhi, The Indian Express reported.
The protest was scheduled for 3:30pm.
A police official said Gandhi was picked up from Bandra and taken to DN Nagar police station. Gandhi claimed on X that he had been arrested and taken to an unknown location. Police denied arresting him, saying he had only been detained.
Guddi S L, vice-president of the organisation, was picked up from Andheri and taken to MIDC police station, police confirmed.
On Friday, Gandhi posted a poster on X urging Mumbaikars to join him at August Kranti Maidan, the site from which the Quit India movement was launched in 1942. The protest was planned in support of the CJP’s demand for the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.
Gamdevi Police said no application had been received or permission granted for the demonstration.
“Due to a Supreme Court ruling, the Mumbai police cannot grant permission to hold a protest at August Kranti Maidan as the land belongs to the Archaeological Survey of India (ASI). No one had approached us in the first instance,” a senior police official said on Friday.
Guddi disputed the claim, saying she had emailed police seeking permission because Gandhi was not in the city but had received no response.
“Gandhi has been called by the police, and they are telling him not to protest. They have also asked him about his location and said that they would detain him,” she said on Friday.
The detentions come amid heightened police vigilance across Maharashtra ahead of the CJP’s planned protest at Jantar Mantar. Police in Mumbai and other parts of the state have been monitoring people suspected of planning to travel to Delhi.
Mumbai Police detained more than 200 people on Friday to prevent them from travelling to the national capital, the report said.

item.title: Two crude bombs hurled outside PM’s Office, police seek suspects
item.description:
Two crude bombs, were hurled outside the Prime Minister’s Office in Tejgaon, Dhaka, early Saturday, prompting police to launch an investigation to identify and arrest those involved.
The incident occurred around 1:15am. One of the bombs exploded, while the other was safely detonated in a controlled explosion by the Bomb Disposal Unit of the Dhaka Metropolitan Police’s (DMP) Counter Terrorism and Transnational Crime (CTTC) unit.
DMP Tejgaon Division Deputy Commissioner Ibne Mizan said police were working to identify and arrest the two suspects who arrived on a motorcycle.
According to him, the two men reached the area around 1:15am, surveyed their surroundings for two to three minutes, hurled the bombs and fled. Police received information that they headed towards Kafrul via Agargaon.
Ibne Mizan said police teams began investigating immediately after the incident. Footage from nearby CCTV cameras has been collected to help identify the suspects, and the incident is being treated as a priority.

item.title: Job seekers block roads in Dhaka over youth development exam paper leak
item.description:
Job seekers blocked several major roads in Dhaka on Saturday to protest the alleged leak of question papers for the Department of Youth Development’s recruitment examination, disrupting traffic in several areas.
Around noon, protesters blocked the road in front of Mirpur Bangla College near the Technical intersection.
Job seekers also took to the streets in Motijheel and at the Aarong intersection in Asad Gate, bringing traffic to a standstill in the affected areas.
The protesters questioned why question paper leaks were still occurring under the current government, recalling that such incidents had also taken place under the previous regime. They questioned the significance of the July 2024 uprising, in which thousands of people sacrificed their lives.
They demanded that the government identify those responsible and ensure exemplary punishment, as well as take strict measures to prevent similar incidents in the future.
Afzal Hossain, a job seeker, said he had travelled hundreds of kilometres from a remote area to Dhaka to sit for the examination.
“After enduring so much hardship to reach the exam centre, I learned that the examination had been postponed because the question paper had been leaked,” he said.
“Who will compensate the thousands of us who went to such lengths to sit for the examination? We demand exemplary punishment for everyone involved in the question paper leak,” he added.

item.title: Humaiun: Bangladesh views Makkah Defence Agreement positively
item.description:
State Minister for Foreign Affairs Humaiun Kobir on Saturday said Bangladesh was positively considering the Makkah Defence Agreement, with any decision to be guided by national interests and the potential contribution of the country's peacekeeping expertise to regional peace and stability.
“We are having positive discussions on the Makkah Defence Agreement. We are viewing it positively,” he said while addressing a national seminar at the Foreign Service Academy in the capital.
Kobir said Bangladesh could take a favourable decision if the agreement served its national interests and its peacekeeping expertise could contribute to the welfare of Muslim nations and help maintain peace and stability in the Middle East.
“If it falls within the national interests of Bangladesh and converges, and we feel that our peacekeeping expertise can add value in serving Muslim nations and keeping a stable, peaceful Middle East, then there is every scope to take a positive decision on the matter,” he said.
The Bangladesh Institute of International and Strategic Studies (BIISS) and the Center for Migration Studies of North South University (NSU) jointly organised the seminar titled “From Workforce to Strategic Partnership: Reimagining Bangladesh-KSA Relations.”
The state minister also said Prime Minister Tarique Rahman had accepted an invitation from Saudi Arabia's Crown Prince to visit the Kingdom.
“He has accepted and will do so at some point very soon,” Kobir said.
He said the Crown Prince had also expressed interest in visiting Bangladesh, adding that Dhaka would welcome him at a mutually convenient time.
Kobir said the proposed visits reflected growing political ties between the two countries. He also described Bangladesh as a strong partner of Saudi Arabia in maritime security.
Calling for a comprehensive economic and strategic partnership, he said bilateral relations should expand beyond their traditional focus on labour migration and remittances.
“While that foundation remains important, it cannot be the ceiling of our ambition,” he said.
He said Saudi Arabia's Vision 2030 and Bangladesh's economic transformation had created common interests in investment, human capital, technology and connectivity.
Discussions were underway on a possible investment fund to facilitate joint investments and partnerships in priority sectors, he added.
The state minister identified renewable energy, infrastructure, ports, logistics, agriculture, fisheries, food security, healthcare, pharmaceuticals, information technology and artificial intelligence as promising areas for Saudi investment.
He said such investments required a predictable and transparent business environment, improved institutional coordination and timely decision-making.
Kobir stressed the need to shift towards trained and certified professionals to meet the changing demands of Saudi Arabia's labour market.
He called for stronger cooperation among training institutions, universities and industries to ensure skills certification aligned with Saudi market requirements.
The welfare, dignity and rights of Bangladeshi workers in Saudi Arabia would remain a government priority, he said.
Kobir also highlighted opportunities for knowledge and technology partnerships, alongside cooperation in ports, shipping, logistics, aviation and supply chains.
“The next chapter of Bangladesh-Saudi Arabia relations should therefore be defined by value creation rather than volume alone,” he said.
Saudi Arabia’s Ambassador to Bangladesh Dr Abdullah Zafer bin Abiyah addressed the seminar as the guest of honour. Foreign Ministry Secretary (Bilateral) Dr Md Nazrul Islam and Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment Secretary Md Mokhtar Ahmed spoke as special guests.
BIISS Director General Major General A S M Ridwanur Rahman and NSU Vice-Chancellor Professor Abdul Hannan Chowdhury also addressed the seminar.
Speaking to journalists after the event, Kobir reiterated that peace and stability in the Middle East and the Muslim world were central to Bangladesh's consideration of the Makkah Defence Agreement.
He said maintaining peace in the region encompassing Makkah and Madinah was a key objective, adding that Bangladesh could deploy its peacekeeping expertise more effectively and extensively across the world.
He said initiatives regarding participation in the agreement or association with the alliance were being considered positively, with regional peace and stability remaining the priority.
Kobir said regular high-level exchanges, including ministerial and official visits in both directions, were strengthening bilateral engagement.
He also stressed the need to diversify employment opportunities into energy, technology and other promising sectors while sending more highly skilled professionals to Saudi Arabia.
“We are also holding very positive discussions with Saudi Arabia and, God willing, many new opportunities will emerge between the two countries,” he said.
The state minister said there was scope for a broad investment partnership under which Bangladesh and Saudi Arabia could jointly invest in profitable sectors.
“The days of dependency are over. We are now placing emphasis on an equal partnership between the two countries and on sustainable policies,” he told journalists.

item.title: Durga Puja festivities begin with observance of Mahalaya
item.description:
Mahalaya, which marks the beginning of Hindu community’s largest religious festival Durga Puja, is being observed across the country amid festivity on Saturday.
From early morning, temples across the country resonated with Chandipath, tarpan rituals, and devotional hymns in praise of Goddess Durga.
The serene autumn dawn ushered in Devipaksha, the fortnight dedicated to the goddess, through the traditional recitation of sacred verses.
Mahalaya that is considered as ceremonial invocation of goddess Durga is observed seven days prior to the initiation of the Durga Puja, the largest religious festival of the Hindu community.
Hindus believe the earth prepares itself and welcomes the coming of the Goddess and her children, through the celebration.
On this day, Hindus remember and pay homage to the deceased ancestors by performing a puja, and offering Brahmins clothes, food and sweets in their name.
From this day, the countdown to Durga Puja begins.
This year, Shashthi Puja will be celebrated on October 17 while Bijoya Dashami on October 21 will mark the goddess’s departure to Kailash.
Scriptures mention three major milestones of Durga Puja—Mahalaya, Bodhon, and Sandhi Puja. On Mahalaya, Goddess Durga receives the divine mandate to defeat the demon king Mahishasura.
Empowered by the combined forces of Brahma, Vishnu, and Shiva, she emerges as `Mahashakti’, adorned with ten weapons and riding a lion, ultimately slaying Mahishasura after a nine-day battle.

Brazil’s Lula scraps gasoline tax ahead of runoff election
item.description:
Brazil’s government announced on Friday that gasoline taxes will be temporarily scrapped, two weeks ahead of the runoff election between incumbent President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and right-wing challenger Flavio Bolsonaro.
Lula, who is seeking his fourth term, is trying to contain rising fuel prices amid a global spike in oil prices driven by the war in the Middle East.
The gasoline tax, which was set at 0.89 reais ($0.18) per liter, would be waived for 30 days, according to the government.
The measure announced on Friday also expands subsidies for importers of diesel, the predominant fuel used in Brazil’s freight transport.
“The objective is to ensure that imports remain viable at a critical moment for supply,” the presidency said in a statement.
The fiscal impact of the tax exemptions will be offset by Brazil’s “extraordinary revenues” from oil exports, it said.
The runoff election on October 25 was set after Lula won 45% of the vote in the first round and Bolsonaro received 47%.
Bolsonaro called his opponent “irresponsible,” warning that Lula was placing a “bomb” on consumers’ laps and that diesel prices could rise after the election.
Bolsonaro, the eldest son of former far-right president Jair Bolsonaro, repeatedly criticized the government during his campaign for failing to control the cost of living.
Inflation in Brazil rose by 0.82% in September, the statistics authority said on Friday.

Barrister Abdul Muntaquim Chaudhury dies at 97
item.description:
Barrister Abdul Muntaquim Chaudhury, a Bangladeshi politician, lawyer and organizer of the Liberation War, died in Melbourne, Australia, on October 9, 2026. He was 97.
Born on September 2, 1929, Chaudhury served as a member of Pakistan’s National Assembly in the 1960s and was re-elected in 1970. After Bangladesh gained independence, he became a member of the Constituent Assembly and helped draft the country’s constitution.
In 1973, he was appointed Bangladesh’s ambassador to Japan. He later served as the country’s ambassador to the German Democratic Republic.
After returning to Bangladesh in 1979, Chaudhury became the founding executive director of the Bangladesh Legal Aid and Services Trust (Blast).
Abu Taher Abdul Muntaquim Chaudhury, whose family descended from the Kanihati Chaudhury family of Sylhet, was the youngest child of Khan Bahadur Tazzammul Ali Chaudhury.
He completed his Intermediate of Arts (IA) at Aligarh Muslim University before studying at Santiniketan and St Xavier’s College. He earned his bachelor’s degree from the University of Calcutta and was later called to the bar at Lincoln’s Inn in London.

item.description:
Dhaka, the overcrowded capital city of Bangladesh, has ranked 4th on the list of cities with the worst air quality, with an AQI index of 181 at 9:06am on Saturday.
Dhaka’s air was classified as "unhealthy", according to the air quality and pollution city ranking.
Singapore, Malaysia’s Kuala Lumpur and India's Kolkata occupied the first, second and third spots in the list, with AQI scores of 200, 198 and 192, respectively.
When the AQI value for particle pollution is between 101 and 150, air quality is considered "unhealthy for sensitive groups", between 150 and 200 is "unhealthy", between 201 and 300 is said to be "very unhealthy", while a reading of 301+ is considered "hazardous", posing serious health risks to residents.
The AQI, an index for reporting daily air quality, informs people how clean or polluted the air of a certain city is and what associated health effects might be a concern for them.
The AQI in Bangladesh is based on five pollutants: particulate matter (PM10 and PM2.5), NO2, CO, SO2, and ozone.
Dhaka has long been grappling with air pollution issues. Its air quality usually turns unhealthy in winter and improves during the monsoon.

Police Additional DIG Tutul Chakraborty dismissed from service
item.description:
The government has dismissed Additional Deputy Inspector General (DIG) of Police Tutul Chakraborty from service after finding him guilty of misconduct, including leaving his post ahead of schedule and using an airport VIP lounge while identifying himself as a “DIG.”
The decision was announced in a notification issued by the Ministry of Home Affairs on Wednesday. According to the notification, Chakraborty was attached to the office of the Rajshahi Range DIG while under suspension and had been “absconding” since January 23.
The notification said Chakraborty had been granted 2 days of leave with permission on November 14 and 15, 2025, followed by 3 days of casual leave from November 16 to 18. However, on November 13, the day before his leave began, he left his post ahead of schedule without submitting the required departure report.
On that day, Chakraborty concealed his identity and introduced himself as a DIG. He then used the DIG lounge and boarded a US-Bangla Airlines flight from Shah Makhdum Airport in Rajshahi to Dhaka at around 10:20am.
The notification further stated that he had used the VIP lounge at Rajshahi Airport several times before, identifying himself as “DIG, Rajshahi Range.” The matter came to the attention of various intelligence agencies, and the notification said his actions had severely damaged the police's image in the eyes of the public.
According to the Ministry of Home Affairs, these actions amounted to gross negligence in performing public duties, disregard for lawful orders and conduct contrary to departmental discipline. Under the Government Employees (Discipline and Appeal) Rules, 2018, the actions constituted “misconduct,” a punishable offense.
A departmental case was filed against Chakraborty over the allegations. On February 5 this year, he was issued a show-cause notice along with a statement of allegations and a charge sheet. However, he did not submit a written reply within the stipulated time or apply for an extension.
The notification said an investigating officer was appointed on April 2 to examine the allegations. Following the investigation, a report was submitted on May 7, concluding that the misconduct charges against Chakraborty had been proven beyond doubt.
Based on the investigation report, a second show-cause notice was issued on June 16, asking why he should not be dismissed from service. He did not respond to that notice either.
The government subsequently reviewed the allegations, the investigation report and other documents before making a preliminary decision to dismiss Chakraborty from service.
The government then sought the opinion of the Bangladesh Public Service Commission, which recommended dismissal on September 14.
The matter was subsequently sent to the president for approval. On October 5, the president approved the dismissal proposal.
Accordingly, Chakraborty has been given the major penalty of dismissal from service under the relevant provisions of the Government Employees (Discipline and Appeal) Rules, 2018.

item.title: Faqir Mahbub calls for global cooperation to ensure children’s online safety
item.description:
Minister of the Ministries for Posts, Telecommunications and Information Technology, and Science and Technology Faqir Mahbub Anam has called for stronger global cooperation, joint initiatives among stakeholders and the exchange of international best practices to ensure children's safety in the digital environment.
He made the call while delivering Bangladesh's statement at the Business IT Breakfast titled "Digital Childhood Without Borders: Best International Practices for Child Safety Online", held in Moscow, Russia, on Thursday.
Representing Bangladesh at the event, the minister also conveyed, on behalf of Prime Minister Tarique Rahman, his appreciation to the Global Digital Forum and the Alliance for the Protection of Children in the Digital Environment for undertaking this timely initiative.
Faqir Mahbub said Bangladesh is undergoing rapid digital transformation, enabling children to benefit from the online world for education and personal development.
At the same time, however, they are increasingly exposed to new and evolving forms of online risks, he added.
Ensuring children's digital safety is no longer the sole responsibility of parents or teachers; rather, it is a shared responsibility involving all stakeholders, including governments, online platforms, technology companies and civil society.
He said that under the leadership of Prime Minister Tarique Rahman, Bangladesh is working to strengthen relevant digital protection laws and legal frameworks, including the Cyber Security Act, to protect children's data and prevent online exploitation.
The minister, however, noted that such challenges cannot be addressed through legislation alone. In this regard, sharing international experiences, best practices and effective solutions that can be implemented on a broad scale is critically important, he said.
Referring to the review of the draft Joint Statement and Terms of Reference of the proposed Global Alliance to Protect Children in the Digital Environment, the minister congratulated the Russian Federation on taking this important initiative.
He further said the proposed document presents a comprehensive, child-rights-based framework in line with the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child.
The minister expressed Bangladesh's strong support for the three core principles of the proposed initiative, saying that the best interests of the child must be given the highest priority, the shared responsibility of all stakeholders must be ensured, and experiences and best practices must be exchanged through international cooperation.
He emphasized the importance of establishing a multilateral stakeholder framework that ensures equitable representation of different geographical regions, including the Asia-Pacific region.
Such a framework would provide opportunities for the realities, challenges and experiences of developing countries like Bangladesh to be appropriately reflected in the formulation of global strategies.
At the same time, Bangladesh welcomes the proposal to establish a Digital Childhood Safety Index and a dedicated platform for research and the exchange of best practices.
Faqir Mahbub Anam said enhancing digital literacy among children, parents and teachers is also a crucial foundation of the initiative.
He observed that developing the necessary knowledge and awareness in line with the rapid advancement of technologies, including artificial intelligence, could help establish an effective preventive mechanism against online harms.
He said Bangladesh remains firmly committed to the principles outlined in the Joint Statement of the Global Alliance to Protect Children in the Digital Environment.
Bangladesh is keen to work closely with the Alliance to protect children from online bullying, sexual harassment, data theft and other forms of digital harm.
The Alliance can play an important role in building a bridge between national policies and global cooperation, he added.
The telecommunications minister said Bangladesh is ready to work with all relevant stakeholders to build a future in which every child, regardless of nationality, can explore the digital world safely, creatively and without fear.
He said the collective initiative was an investment in future generations and that the digital future being built must be not only connected but also safe, inclusive and child-friendly.
Representatives from more than 100 countries participated in the international forum.

item.title: UK parliamentary delegation meets political and civil society leaders
item.description:
The British All-Party Parliamentary Group (APPG) on Bangladesh has held a series of high-level meetings with political and civil society leaders during its visit to Bangladesh this week.

It subsequently met Deputy Speaker Barrister Kayser Kamal MP at the Bangladesh Parliament and held meetings at ministerial offices with Minister Humaiun Kobir, Minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury MP and Adviser Rashed Al Mahmud Titumir.

On Thursday, the delegation met President Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir at Bangabhaban. Discussions covered women's representation in Parliament, the July Charter and constitutional change, political party reform, training and development for parliamentarians, and truth and reconciliation processes for historical rights abuses.
The delegation also met Minister for Cultural Affairs Nitin Roy Chowdhury MP and Nipun Roy Chowdhury MP at the minister's offices.
Further meetings have been held with opposition leaders and civil society figures.
The delegation also visited the offices of BRAC and the BRAC Institute for Governance and Development, as well as the Drik Picture Library. ‘Mental health awareness remains a major challenge’
item.description:
On the occasion of World Mental Health Day, Professor Dr Saifun Nahar, director of the National Institute of Mental Health and Hospital, spoke to Dhaka Tribune about Bangladesh’s mental health situation, healthcare services, social stigma, mental health among children and adolescents, and suicide prevention.
Dr Saifun Nahar: According to the National Mental Health Survey 2019, the prevalence of mental health problems among adults in Bangladesh is 18.7%, while the rate among children and adolescents is 12.6%. Among people aged 60 and above, 28% experience mental health problems.
Patients with various mental health conditions visit our outpatient and inpatient departments, where we provide treatment for almost all types of mental health problems.
Among children, online gaming addiction, gambling-related problems, internet addiction and mobile phone addiction are becoming increasingly common.
There are different types of mental health problems, which can broadly be classified into neurotic and psychotic disorders. Changes in brain functioning can affect a person's thoughts, emotions, behaviour and daily life.
As a result, their ability to function in their personal, professional, family and social lives may deteriorate. In general, changes in one's daily activities and functioning can help indicate a potential problem.
A mentally healthy person can generally maintain normal functioning and productivity in their work, communication, social interactions and other activities. Significant changes in these areas, however, may indicate a mental health problem.
Many people with psychotic disorders have limited awareness of their condition, and their judgement may also become impaired. Consequently, they may not recognise the need for treatment.
People experiencing neurotic disorders, on the other hand, can often identify changes in themselves. These may include mood swings, a loss of interest in routine activities, difficulty completing tasks or a decline in the quality of their work.
Mental health problems can also manifest as physical symptoms, including loss of appetite, headaches, body aches and digestive problems. They may also affect sexual desire or functioning.
The mind and body are closely connected, and mental health problems can also affect physical health. For example, many patients with depression experience various physical aches and pains. Anxiety-related disorders can cause palpitations, digestive problems and headaches.
Anyone experiencing a mental health problem should seek medical attention. However, when relatives or neighbours learn that someone is receiving mental health treatment, the person may sometimes face social humiliation. We must move away from these superstitions and prejudices. Unless we break this taboo, we will not be able to address the problem effectively.
There are also many misconceptions about mental health. Some people believe that counselling alone is enough to ensure recovery, that medication must be taken for life once treatment begins, that mental illnesses are incurable, or that psychiatric medication damages the brain. We must work to dispel these misconceptions.
Patients can recover with appropriate treatment and medication taken as prescribed by a doctor. We must also strengthen public trust in doctors and mental health services.
More than 500 patients visit our outpatient department every day. Our inpatient department has 400 beds. At times, all the beds are occupied, while on other occasions, occupancy is around 80%.
We are working to improve our services further. The current government is also taking initiatives to advance mental health services.
Our mental health workforce is still inadequate. However, compared with the past, more talented students are choosing to study this subject. We have introduced four additional courses in response to growing interest in the field. At the same time, the workforce is gradually expanding.
Children experience different types of mental health problems depending on their age. Among children and adolescents, we see cases of autism spectrum disorder, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), internet addiction, gaming addiction and mobile phone addiction.
Many children are also developing problematic patterns of pornography use. Drug addiction is another concern among street children, with some becoming increasingly involved in glue sniffing and the use of readily available drugs such as yaba.
A coordinated approach is needed to address mental health problems among children and adolescents. Conflict and other forms of pressure within the family can affect a child's mental well-being. When children regularly witness arguments between their parents, their cognitive development may be affected, and they may develop trust issues later in life.
If they struggle to manage anger and stress, they may also become vulnerable to suicidal thoughts or behaviour.
Similarly, children who experience bullying or humiliation at school, or face excessive academic pressure, may develop various mental health problems that can affect them later in life.
People with certain personality disorders, particularly those with abrasive personality traits, may exhibit suicidal behaviour. People living with various mental illnesses, including those experiencing hallucinations or delusions, may also develop suicidal tendencies. Drug addiction can also increase the risk of suicide.
Awareness is crucial in this regard. Suicide can be prevented by identifying mental health problems early and ensuring that those affected receive appropriate treatment and support.
Mental health services have expanded compared with the situation 10 years ago. Through the World Health Organization's mental health programme, doctors from different districts and upazilas are receiving training to help reduce gaps in treatment services.
Doctors from areas outside major urban centres are brought in for training. After returning to their respective workplaces, they pass on their knowledge and train other healthcare professionals.
There may not be dedicated posts for psychiatrists at district- or upazila-level health complexes. However, doctors working in these areas are being trained to provide primary mental healthcare to patients. After completing their training, they return to their respective areas and provide services there.
Regardless of the cause of an illness, anyone who is unwell should receive appropriate treatment. Whether mental health problems stem from personal circumstances, family issues or other factors, seeking treatment is essential.
Sometimes, people do not realise that they are experiencing a mental health problem. In such cases, family members and relatives should help them seek professional care by taking them to a psychiatrist and arranging the necessary counselling or other treatment.
The government has already undertaken various projects to strengthen community mental health teams. The integration of mental health services into primary healthcare was included in earlier initiatives, and the programme is now being advanced further.
One year is a very short time, and it is not possible to resolve all the challenges within that period. The treatment gap remains substantial. Among adults, it is 92%, while among children, it is 95%.
This means that only 8% of adults who need mental health services are receiving them, while the remaining 92% are not. Among children who need such services, only 5% receive them, leaving 95% without access to the care they need.
If everyone works together, we can bring about positive changes. However, resolving all these problems within a single year is not possible. We are continuing our efforts to improve the situation.
Public awareness remains inadequate, and many people do not give mental health the importance it deserves. Much of the problem can be addressed if people take mental illness seriously and seek treatment when necessary.
Individuals, families, educational institutions and the state must all work together to raise awareness, reduce stigma and ensure that people with mental health conditions receive appropriate care.

People to bid final farewell to Toufique Imrose Khalidi Saturday
item.description:
People from all walks of life will pay their last respects to Toufique Imrose Khalidi, editor-in-chief of bdnews24.com and a pioneer of digital journalism in Bangladesh who died in London, on Saturday afternoon.
His body will arrive in Bangladesh from the United Kingdom on Saturday morning.
The coffin will then be taken to his residence, where family members and relatives will pay their last respects.
The body will be kept at the Banani Old DOHS playground from 2:00pm to 3:00pm, where friends, relatives, colleagues, well-wishers and representatives from different sectors of society will pay their final tributes.
His namaz-e-janaza will be held at the same venue at 3:00pm and later Toufique Imrose Khalidi will be laid to rest at the Martyred Intellectuals Graveyard in Mirpur at 5:00pm.
Meanwhile, his son Rad Sharar Khalidi has urged people across the country to pray for his father's eternal peace.
Toufique Imrose Khalidi passed away at a hospital in London on October 2 at the age of 59 following brain haemorrhage.
Born on June 14, 1967, Khalidi earned his master's degree in English Literature from Dhaka University before embarking on a career in journalism in 1989 with The Sunday Express.
Over a career spanning more than three decades, he held key positions across national and international media. He worked at the BBC World Service in London from February 2000 to June 2005.
Prior to that, he served at The Daily Star as Joint News Editor and Weekend Edition News Editor (1998-2000), Business Editor (1997-1998), and Diplomatic Correspondent (1991-1993), as well as Assistant Editor and Senior Correspondent at The Financial Express.
In the first half of 2005, Toufique Imrose Khalidi associated with bdnews24.com, pioneering Bangladesh's first internet-based 24/7 news service.
He received fellowships from the Journalists in Europe Foundation in Paris and the Japan Foreign Press Centre.
In 2014, he was named one of the “14 leading digital media innovators” across Asia-Pacific, Latin America, and West Asia at the South-to-South Media Dialogue in South Africa.
Toufique Imrose Khalidi chaired a UNESCO World Press Freedom Day event in 2016, attended the 2009 UN Climate Conference in Copenhagen as an observer, participated in the Global Media Forum in Bonn (2010, 2016, 2017, 2019), and spoke as a panelist at Harvard University’s "Bangladesh Rising" conference in 2018.
He also played a vital role in national policy formulation, serving on national committees for online media policy (2012, 2015), the news agency policy committee (2008), and the national task force for Dhaka river protection (2007).
In December 2017, the Bangladesh government conferred a special award on him on National ICT Day.

item.title: Bangladesh snatch late winner to beat Uzbekistan in U17 qualifiers
item.description:
Bangladesh scored a last-gasp goal to secure a 2-1 win against Uzbekistan in their AFC U17 Women’s Asian Cup China 2027 Qualifiers Group H match on Thursday.
Bangladesh will face off against the Philippines on Sunday to decide who will advance to the finals with Uzbekistan eliminated.
Uzbekistan, who lost 4-0 to the Philippines on Monday, knew they had to get something from this match to stay in the hunt for a place in the Finals but it was Bangladesh who drew first blood.
In the fourth minute, Fatema Akter swung a diagonal cross halfway across the pitch to Purnima Marma on the right flank, who then drew Mariya Khalkulova out of her goal before chipping the ball past the advancing keeper for the opener.
Bangladesh, however, undid their good work in the 17th minute when Airin Khatun dallied on the edge of her box, allowing Larangiz Lakaeva to dispossess her before slotting past Meghla Rani Roy.
The second half was evenly matched with both teams working hard to carve out chances.
Alpi Akter went close for the Tigresses when she dribbled into the box from the right but saw her effort saved by Khalkulova while at the other end, Meghla did well to parry Mubina Bakhtiyorova’s attempt from close range.
As Uzbekistan pushed forward late on, Bangladesh exploited the gaps in defence in the third minute of added time when Sorovi Rani sent Runa Akter through on goal to power home the winning goal.

item.title: Trump rules out new Iran attack before US midterm elections
item.description:
President Donald Trump on Thursday ruled out attacking Iran before the US midterm elections on November 3, saying Washington was holding "productive discussions" with Tehran.
Trump's post on his Truth Social platform followed a surge in oil prices on Thursday driven by media reports suggesting potential new US strikes prior to those elections.
"I want to make it clear to everybody that, while Iran is in very bad condition, both Economically and Militarily, and while the Blockade will remain in full force and effect...we will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the Midterm Elections," he wrote.
"We are having productive discussions with the Islamic Republic of Iran," he added, without providing additional details.
The Atlantic magazine reported on Wednesday that the White House had asked the Pentagon to develop options to strike Iranian targets that could be used before the midterms. The New York Times published a similar report on Thursday, saying the plans were being developed despite Trump's "ambivalence."
The rise in crude oil prices has also been fueled by persistent tensions in the Strait of Hormuz -- a strategic chokepoint for the global oil trade -- as well as hostilities between Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis and Saudi Arabia.
Polls suggest that US voters are strongly dissatisfied over rising fuel prices, linked to the conflict launched by the United States and Israel against Iran on February 28.
Brent North Sea crude, the international benchmark, rallied to as high as $105.88 a barrel before retreating to $104.28.
Meanwhile, Russian President Vladimir Putin promised Thursday to "do everything" to help end the Middle East war when he met Iranian counterpart Masoud Pezeshkian for talks ahead of a regional summit, Russian media reported.
"We are ready to do everything that is in our power to contribute to the settlement of this situation," Putin said after arriving in Turkmenistan for a summit of the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) that starts Friday in the Caspian Sea resort of Avaza.
He added that Iran had made "real efforts to end the war," according to Russian news agencies.
Russia and Iran have reinforced diplomatic and military links since Russia launched its offensive in Ukraine in February 2022, becoming increasingly reliant on each other.
Trump has repeatedly insisted in recent weeks that the United States has effectively won the Iran war, despite ongoing unrest and a recent security threat that forced the withdrawal of American bombers from a base in England.
But Trump's claims that prices will fall as soon as the Iran war is over have so far fallen on deaf ears with voters.
The midterm elections will shape the final two years of Trump's presidential term as his Republican Party risks losing its current grip on Congress.
Although Trump is not on the ballot, he is holding numerous rallies in an attempt to limit the damage or even turn the political tide.
Trump has warned he faces a possible third impeachment if Democrats retake the House of Representatives, and the White House is preparing for a slew of investigations into corruption and abuse of power.
The US president also on Thursday sought to calm a furor over his comments at a rally earlier this week that Iran could "take out" the cities of Los Angeles and San Diego.
Trump, 80, blamed the "fake and artificial news" for misinterpreting the remarks, which Democrats pounced on.
"In actuality, what I was talking about was that a temporary increase in the price of Gasoline is a small price to pay for Iran not having a Nuclear Weapon and, if you want to see a big price, can you imagine what it would be like if they bombed San Diego and/or Los Angeles?" Trump said on Truth Social.

item.title: From Aibak’s horse messengers to the digital age: Rebirthing the post
item.description:
As the world celebrates World Post Day on October 9, many might assume that the relevance of postal services has faded in an era of instantaneous digital messages that travel thousands of miles at the touch of a fingertip.
Thanks to technology-induced transformations and value-added services, today we celebrate a global system that does far more than just deliver mail.
With over 660,000 post offices and 4.6 million staff across the globe, the postal network connects communities and provides essential services designed to leave no one behind.
This year’s theme, “One postal network, infinite possibilities,” reflects the role of the postal system as a trusted facilitator and a one-stop shop enabling people to participate in the economy and society—whether it is a young person opening a digital bank account, a family accessing virtual healthcare, a small business reaching global markets, or an elderly neighbor receiving a welfare check.
Crucially, these services are delivered in person, providing a real, human touchpoint in an increasingly digital world. As one of the oldest examples of multilateralism, global cooperation ensures messages and goods arrive even amid disasters, prompting United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres to invite the world to honor postal workers and the Universal Postal Union for all they do to connect our world.
“The postal system is one of the oldest examples of multilateralism in action, with global cooperation ensuring messages, goods and services arrive even amid disasters and emergencies. Today, let’s honour postal workers and the Universal Postal Union – and all they do to connect our world,” the UN Secretary-General says in message marking the day.
In Bangladesh, the Directorate of Posts is observing a nationwide Postal Service Week from today, featuring letter festivals, philatelic exhibitions, and postal fairs at educational institutions to engage the younger generation. As the nation joins the global observance of World Post Day 2026, the department is actively transforming its traditional operations into a modern, technology-driven logistics network.
The roots of this system trace back to the 13th century, when Qutb ud-Din Aibak, the Turkic general who founded the Delhi Sultanate, established the first recorded postal network in Bengal using horse messengers from Delhi. The system was further developed by Sultan Muhammad bin Tughluq, as noted by Arabian travel writer Ibn Battuta, when postal officers also engaged in law enforcement. Further improvements were made under Sher Shah Suri, founder of the Suri Empire, who developed the Grand Trunk Road and established 1,700 postal houses with 3,400 runners, while Mughal Emperor Jahangir later introduced carrier pigeons to transport messages.
Following the East India Company’s takeover of Bengal, Robert Clive established a General Post Office in Kolkata on March 17, 1774, creating a network known as Clive’s Post that connected commercial hubs like Calcutta, Chittagong, Dhaka, Dinajpur, Murshidabad, Rajshahi, Rangpur, and Rajmahal. On October 1, 1854, the first postage stamps worth one anna and half anna were introduced, followed by the adoption of rail transport that same year and the launch of the Railway Mail Service in 1864. Roadside letter boxes were introduced between 1856 and 1857.
During the 1971 Liberation War, the provisional government established a postal service with 50 field offices near the Indian border in Mukti Bahini-controlled areas. Barrister Moudud Ahmed served as the first Postmaster General, and artist Biman Mullick designed the nation’s first eight stamps—including one featuring Sheikh Mujibur Rahman—which were subsequently outlawed by the Pakistani government.
Today, that historic framework has expanded into a vast network of over 8,000 post offices employing roughly 40,000 staff across Bangladesh. Faced with a sharp decline in personal correspondence—with annual mail volumes plummeting from over 400 million letters in the 1980s and 1990s to less than 50 million today—the department must realign its deliverables with tech-driven platforms to utilize its full potential.
According to its official site, the Bangladesh Post Office currently caters to 16 types of services, including ordinary and registered mail, Guaranteed Express Post, Express Mail Service, ordinary money orders, Electronic Money Transfer Service, postal cash cards, parcel services, Value Payable Post, Value Payable Letters, postage stamp sales, postal life insurance, savings banks, savings certificate operations, prize bond management, biri banderol printing, and the distribution of non-postal government stamps.
According to a recent ministry press release, the scope of these services is expanding through enhanced e-commerce capabilities, digital tracking, post pickup services, fulfillment centers, specialized transport for agricultural products, and entrepreneur-based franchise post offices.
Recent data shows that around 811 tonnes of goods have been transported via Speed Post since March 2026, making it an affordable lifeline for online businesses, farmers, and small enterprises. International parcel transportation is also growing; outbound volumes rose from 243 tonnes in the first three months of the 2025–26 fiscal year to 316 tonnes during the same period in the 2026–27 fiscal year, marking a 29.84 percent increase.
Furthermore, the postal service recently played a vital civic role by ensuring the exercise of voting rights through postal ballots for 1,533,683 expatriate and domestic voters during the 13th parliamentary election in February 2026, proving that this centuries-old institution remains deeply relevant to modern society.

item.title: DNCC launches campaign to repaint July graffiti on metro rail pillars

item.title: Police: DNA from crime-scene matches two accused in Rangpur family murder
item.description:
The DNA of the two suspects arrested in connection with the murders of former schoolteacher Ganapati Chakraborty and his family members in Rangpur has shown a “statistical match” to DNA collected from different pieces of evidence found at the scene, police have said.
Samples collected from date seeds, bitten cucumber pieces and cigarette filters found at the spot showed a match in laboratory tests, Rangpur Metropolitan Police Deputy Commissioner (Detective Branch) Sonaton Chakroborty said on Thursday night.
“Tests on the DNA samples collected from Siddhartha Das and Mugdha Das at the CID Forensic Lab in Dhaka matched the DNA found in the evidence,” he said.
According to sources, forensic tests had earlier detected male DNA in the date seeds, cucumber pieces and cigarette filters, but investigators had yet to identify whose DNA it was. The samples were subsequently compared with those collected from the two suspects.
On August 22, the bodies of Ganapati, 65, a former teacher of Rangpur Zilla School, his wife Pritilata Chakraborty Bala, 50, daughter Agami Chakraborty Prarthi, 25, and son Ayush Chakraborty Priyam, 12, were recovered from their locked home in Machhuapara of Rangpur city.
Within six hours of the murders, police arrested two suspects, Mugdha and Siddharth.
The two suspects were taken from Rangpur Central Jail to Dhaka on the night of September 20, and their DNA samples were collected at the Criminal Investigation Department (CID) office the following day.
Investigators collected more than 35 pieces of evidence from the scene, including a fruit knife, foil used for Yaba consumption, cigarette ends, cucumbers, dates, marks on a washbasin and writing found in a notebook belonging to one of the deceased children.
The items were sent for forensic examination in several phases.
Police had earlier said the suspects stayed inside the house after the killings and ate dates and cucumbers.
The DB is investigating the incident.

Malaysia closes schools in capital, parts of country due to haze
item.description:
Malaysia closed schools in Kuala Lumpur and other parts of the country on Friday, as haze from fires in neighboring Indonesia again plunged local air quality to among the world’s worst.
Toxic smoke from peatland as well as forest fires has shrouded towns and cities in the region for more than a month, sending respiratory complaints skyrocketing.
The school closures came as Malaysia’s leader discussed the choking smoke with his Indonesian counterpart and called for an urgent regional meeting.
Kuala Lumpur’s air quality worsened on Friday to hit a reading of around 224 on the index of Swiss-based monitor IQAir, which said that change pushed Malaysia’s capital past Singapore to be the “most polluted global major city.”
Malaysia’s Education Minister Fadhlina Sidek said she has instructed full school closures in four states and two federal territories as well as one partial closure in the central Pahang State.
Schools were also closed on Friday in three districts in western Perak State.
Malaysia’s education ministry could not immediately be reached for comment on whether schools will reopen on Monday.
“In the future, we will ensure that any decision to close schools is notified in advance so that parents have sufficient time to prepare,” Fadhlina said late on Thursday.
Malaysia’s King Sultan Ibrahim weighed in on the matter on Thursday, saying schools should be closed as air quality readings reached 150 or higher on the Air Pollutant Index (API).
“Appropriate measures must be taken by the relevant ministries and agencies to protect schoolchildren and students, including senior citizens and patients with respiratory illnesses,” King Sultan Ibrahim said.
Under Malaysian guidelines, API readings above 100 are classified as unhealthy, above 200 as very unhealthy, above 300 as hazardous, while readings beyond 500 constitute the threshold for declaring a local emergency.
Malaysia’s Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said Thursday he discussed the fire situation with the Indonesian leader Prabowo Subianto.
“The haze issue is indeed at a worrying level. And I have personally contacted President Prabowo,” Anwar said.
“And he also agreed to take the necessary steps,” Anwar said, without going into specific details.
He said Malaysia has been taking measures to combat the haze, including increasing attempts to trigger rain via cloud seeding.
Indonesia’s government said “regular dialogue between the leaders is a natural part of the close relations” of the two nations.
Experts said the flames are being fanned by a turbo-charged El Nino weather phenomenon, causing the worst pollution conditions in years.
Anwar said he asked Malaysia’s Foreign Minister Mohamad Hasan to contact the 11-nation Association of Southeast Asian Nations’ secretariat for an urgent meeting between environmental ministers to discuss the matter.
“So these are all the steps we are taking, but we are monitoring and will try the measures that we ought to take next,” Anwar said.
Singapore’s air quality levels too dipped into the “very unhealthy” range with a reading of 209 on the Air Quality Index in Friday afternoon, according to the IQAir website.
The AQI converts measurements of pollutants into a single figure indicating air quality and potential health risks.
Readings above 150 are classified as unhealthy, while levels above 300 are considered hazardous.

item.title: UN calls for inclusive mental health care on World Mental Health Day
item.description:
The United Nations has reaffirmed the expertise and leadership of people with lived experience of mental health challenges on World Mental Health Day.
This year’s theme, “Lived Experiences Heard: Real Voices, Real Change,” highlights how people are often excluded from decisions affecting their lives, despite their insights being essential to developing effective services and policies.
The UN said it is particularly important for young people facing economic uncertainty, climate anxiety and online harms, as well as people affected by conflicts and humanitarian crises, where disrupted services can worsen psychological distress.
More than 80% of countries currently provide mental health services in psychiatric hospitals, while many people with lived experience prefer to recover at home and in their communities, it said.
The UN has further called on governments to replace exclusion with partnership and invest in community-centred mental health care.
It has also urged renewed efforts to address stigma and build mental health systems grounded in dignity and human rights for all.

item.title: US: Bangladesh steps up anti-trafficking efforts but gaps persist
item.description:
The government of Bangladesh convicted fewer traffickers and did not take adequate steps to address internal trafficking crimes, which remained pervasive, said the United States in its latest report released on Thursday.
The government of Bangladesh does not fully meet the minimum standards for the elimination of trafficking but is making significant efforts to do so, said the report.
The government demonstrated overall increasing efforts compared with the previous reporting period; therefore, Bangladesh remained on Tier 2, the report said.
These efforts included passing the Prevention and Suppression of Human Trafficking and Smuggling of Migrants Ordinance 2026 to strengthen the legal framework to combat trafficking, increasing investigations and prosecutions, updating the human trafficking crime and victim identification guidelines, and piloting a digital NRM to increase timeliness and coordination of referrals to protection services.
The government also strengthened protections for migrant workers to reduce vulnerabilities to trafficking.
However, the government did not meet the minimum standards in several key areas.
The government identified fewer victims, and victim protection and reintegration efforts remained insufficient, particularly for Rohingya refugees and returning Bangladeshi migrant workers.
Additionally, the government continued to permit worker-paid recruitment fees that rendered many migrant workers indebted, increasing their vulnerability to trafficking.
Spokesman at the US Department of State Thomas Tommy Pigott said human trafficking is a direct assault on the values of freedom and dignity that define America.
The 2026 Trafficking in Persons Report reveals new ways criminal organizations and repressive regimes use this abhorrent practice for financial gain.
The report also called for accountability for governments that fail to punish traffickers and protect their citizens.
The Trump Administration will use all available tools to fight traffickers and their enablers and bring them to justice, said the spokesman.

item.title: Dhaka air 5th worst in world Friday morning
item.description:
Dhaka ranked 5th among the world's most polluted cities on Friday morning, recording an Air Quality Index (AQI) score of 172 at 9:15am.
The air quality was classified as ‘unhealthy’, meaning the concentration of pollutants in the air had reached a level that could pose health risks to the general population, according to the AQI scale.
Singapore in Singapore ranked first with an AQI score of 217, while Kuala Lumpur in Malaysia ranked second with a score of 210, followed by Lahore in Pakistan in third place with an AQI score of 186.
According to AQI standards, a reading between 101 and 150 is considered 'unhealthy for sensitive groups', while 151 to 200 is classified as 'unhealthy'. A reading between 201 and 300 is considered 'very unhealthy', while levels above 301 are deemed 'hazardous', posing serious health risks.
The AQI provides daily updates on air quality, indicating how clean or polluted the air is and highlighting potential health impacts.
In Bangladesh, the AQI is calculated based on five major pollutants: particulate matter (PM10 and PM2.5), nitrogen dioxide (NO2), carbon monoxide (CO), sulfur dioxide (SO2), and ozone.
Dhaka has long struggled with air pollution, with air quality typically deteriorating during winter and improving during the monsoon season.
The World Health Organization estimates that air pollution causes around seven million deaths globally each year, mainly from stroke, heart disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, lung cancer and acute respiratory infections.

Fired researchers accuse OpenAI of 'chilling' safety efforts
item.description:
Three former OpenAI security researchers on Thursday accused the ChatGPT-maker of firing them for warning about the dangers of artificial intelligence, reigniting the debate over safety at a company whose software has been involved in security breaches.
"I believe we were fired for prioritizing safety over the near-term interests of OpenAI as a corporation," one of the fired staffers, Mikita Balesni, wrote on X, breaking a weeklong silence since their very public dismissal.
Balesni and the two other fired employees, Tomek Korbak and Jasmine Wang, publicly shared a letter to OpenAI on Thursday.
"Our firing leaves us worried that the norms inside OpenAI are shifting," the letter says, and continues that "terminations such as ours, executed and communicated so abruptly, are chilling the open culture OpenAI has prized in the past."
They also call on the company to keep its promise to permanently host independent auditors.
"We are concerned that our firings may be used to justify ending" that work, the letter says.
OpenAI, for its part, said it fired them for allegedly violating company rules.
"Our investigation confirmed that these individuals mishandled sensitive information outside established company procedures, violating our policies and breaking the trust essential to our work," OpenAI told AFP in a statement on October 1.
"We do not terminate employees for raising concerns," a research executive at OpenAI said in a memo to staff on Wednesday, an excerpt of which was shared with AFP.
The three fired researchers worked on monitoring OpenAI's models, which escaped their testing environment in July and hacked Hugging Face, an AI coding library.
The incident sparked a heated debate in Silicon Valley over whether or not to slow the development of this technology.
If OpenAI's researchers can no longer sound the alarm or work with outside parties, "we are all at greater risk that something truly catastrophic will happen," the researchers' letter warns.
They also claim that nearly 400 OpenAI employees signed a petition in July that called for an industry-wide slowdown on advanced development of AI models.
In September, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and SpaceX chief Elon Musk called for a slowdown as well.
"Right now we're investing more in safety, security, alignment, monitoring and that will allow us to continue to progress model capability a lot," Altman told reporters last month.
Others, like Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, want to move full steam ahead.
US regulators are unlikely to intervene.
Last month, President Donald Trump hosted a group of American tech executives who agreed to abide by a voluntary code of conduct on AI safety.
